title: Platform Management
overview: Platform management keeps interactions scalable, available and safe to change. This topic covers discovery, deployment strategies, circuit breakers, rate limits, tracing, sagas, metrics and centralised logs. Practise choosing a tool from the failure it prevents and explaining the assumptions behind its guarantees.
big_ideas: A platform's value is the producer-consumer interaction; engineering scales, limits, measures and evolves it.
Service discovery registers names and locations, resolves a target, then connects. Keep discovery infrastructure available; consensus-backed registries commonly use 3 or 5 nodes.
Blue/green switches environments; rolling gradually replaces instances; canary limits live exposure; shadowing mirrors requests and discards new-version responses.
Circuit breaker is a state machine (Closed, Open, Half-Open) that fails fast to stop cascading failures; rate limiting caps callers using an in-memory quota store.
Distributed tracing passes a UUID via headers; a trace spans services, a span is one unit of work.
Sagas replace 2PC with local transactions plus compensations (orchestrated or choreographed) but offer no read isolation.
Distinguish time-based uptime, request success (yield) and reachable data (harvest). Use the lecture’s stated uptime formula when requested, with its denominator assumption explicit.
Prefer platform features (Kubernetes DNS, Istio, ELK/Prometheus) over hand-coded plumbing.

sections.title: Why engineers care: the platform toolbox
sections.summary: A platform exists to enable producer-consumer interaction, and engineering's job is a toolbox that scales, protects and evolves that interaction.

notes.h: Platform = business model; engineering makes it work
items: **Creates value** by facilitating exchanges between interdependent groups (**consumers** and **producers**)

sub: data and APIs for a health agency

items: Modern platforms **blur infrastructure and application architecture**
notes.foot: Engineering is what makes the platform's interactions work.

items: **Scalability** → increasing and limiting interaction
**Availability** → a seamless experience
**Evolvability** → shipping fixes and features
notes.foot: These decide whether the platform survives: a **consistently bad experience kills a platform**.

notes.h: Toolbox maps tools to business intent
items: **Service discovery**
**Deployment strategies** (canary, rolling)
**Circuit breaker** and **rate limiting**
**Distributed tracing**
**Metrics collection**
**Log aggregation**
notes.foot: Together they **scale** the interaction, **limit** it, **measure** it, and let you **enhance the platform without disrupting users**.

terms.def: A business model that creates value by facilitating exchanges between producers and consumers.

check.q: A product manager calls deployment strategies and distributed tracing 'ops plumbing' and wants the platform team on features only. How do you argue for them?

a.lead: A platform's value is the **interaction between producers and consumers**; a consistently bad experience drives both away. The toolbox protects that interaction:
items: **Scalability**: increasing and limiting it
**Availability**: a seamless experience
**Evolvability**: releasing fixes and features safely
**Data** to improve it
a.foot: Features nobody can use during outages or slow fixes do not grow the platform.

check.q: Map each tool to the business intent it serves: canary releases, rate limiting and distributed tracing.

items: **Canary releases** → experimentation and seamless rollout = **evolvability** without disrupting users
**Rate limiting** → **limits the interaction**, protecting scarce resources and spending from excessive or abusive traffic
**Distributed tracing** → lowers **reaction time** when something breaks → shortens recovery, protects **availability**

sections.title: Service discovery
sections.summary: How services find each other when instances come and go: a registry that works like an internal DNS, kept highly available by a consensus cluster.

items: **Monolith** → operationally simpler, but scales and deploys as a unit
**SOA and microservices** → add service boundaries and reuse
**Microservices** → favour independent scaling, deployment and data ownership, with greater operational overhead
**Containers** are a common implementation of microservices, not their definition

notes.h: Why hardcoded IPs fail in the cloud
items: **Auto-scaling** creates new instances that must join load balancing
**Nodes or containers restart and move** (fallacies of distributed computing)
**Survive node failures**
**Store service locations**
**Spare clients from using raw IPs**
**Not a single point of failure**

notes.lead: As on the internet (DNS), look services up by name.
items: **Service registry** = effectively an internal DNS server
**East-west traffic** → service to service inside the platform (what the registry serves)
**North-south traffic** → users to platform
**Register** the service (name to IP)
**Look it up** from the registry
**Connect** to it
**Consensus-backed registries** → ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul
Commonly use **3 or 5 nodes**
A **majority must agree** on changes
**3 nodes** tolerates one unavailable node; **5 nodes** tolerates two
**Even-sized clusters** can form a majority, but an extra even-numbered member does not increase failure tolerance
**Kubernetes** (lecture example) → callers use a service alias such as http://payment-manager-service:8080
In Kubernetes, **service registration and DNS integration are platform-managed**
**Spring Cloud/Eureka** example → requires more application integration
notes.foot: Prefer a **supported platform capability** over duplicating plumbing.

terms.def: Traffic between services inside the platform.
Traffic between users and the platform.
Internal DNS-like store of service names and locations.
Paxos/Raft/ZAB: keeps registry cluster nodes agreeing (ZooKeeper, etcd, consul).

check.q: During a traffic spike, auto-scaling adds six new instances of the Payment service, but the callers are configured with the two original IP addresses. What happens, and what is the fix?

a.lead: **All traffic still goes to the two original instances.**
items: **New instances sit idle** → the spike is not absorbed
**Original instance restarts at a new address** → calls to it fail

items.t: **Fix: service registry**: callers refer to Payment by an **alias** resolved through it
sub: Works like an **internal DNS**: instances **register**, callers **look up**, then **connect**

a.foot: The registry must itself be **highly available**.

check.q: A team wants a four-node service-registry cluster 'for extra safety' instead of three. Do you agree?

items: **Consensus protocol** (Raft or Paxos) needs a **majority**
**4 nodes** → need 3 votes → still tolerate only **1 failure**, the same as **3 nodes**
**5 nodes** → tolerate **2**
a.foot: The fourth node adds cost and coordination without adding failure tolerance → hence **odd sizes** such as three or five are the norm.

check.q: Services run on a container orchestrator with built-in DNS-based discovery. A teammate wants to add a library-based registry with client and server code as well. Advise.

a.lead: **Use the built-in DNS**, not a library-based registry.
items: **Built-in DNS** already provides **registration and lookup by alias**, with no discovery code in the services
**Library-based registry** needs **client and server code** → takes engineers away from **business requirements**
**A second registry** = another component to keep **highly available**
a.foot: Add one only if some services run **outside the orchestrator** and must be discovered the same way.

steps.label: 1. Register
steps.detail: On start-up each service (e.g. payment-service at 192.168.4.12) registers its alias and address with the service registry.

steps.label: 2. Lookup
steps.detail: The calling service (e.g. Agency) refers to the callee by alias and gets the current IP from the registry, like a DNS lookup.

steps.label: 3. Connect
steps.detail: With the address in hand the caller connects to the service. The registry is not in the data path.

sections.title: Deployment strategies
sections.summary: Four ways to release a new version (blue/green, rolling, canary, shadowing) and when to choose each.

notes.h: Pick a strategy from business context
items: **Downtime tolerance** → how tolerant are customers of downtime (nines; banks, e-commerce)?
**Global users**? Are users global?
**Release frequency** → how often do you release?
**Rollback speed** → how fast can you roll back?
**Experiment in production**? (A/B tests, passive machine learning models)
**Blue/green** → keeps old and new environments available and switches live traffic
**Rolling** → progressively replaces old instances
**Canary** → a small share of live requests goes to the new version (lecture uses **5–10%**)
**Shadowing** → sends copies to the new version but discards its responses
Only a **small set of users or servers** sees the release
Must be **incremental** and **backward compatible** for easy rollback
**Gradually replace instances** while others serve traffic
**Avoid duplicating a full environment**
**Temporary extra capacity** may still be needed
notes.foot: **"No downtime" is a design goal**, not an automatic property.

items: **Rolling** → compatible routine patches
**Canary** → limited real-user exposure
**Blue/green** → fast traffic switch-back while both environments remain ready
**Shadowing** → compares behaviour without returning new responses; **mirrored writes must be isolated** to avoid duplicate side effects

terms.def: Two full environments; switch over once the new one is verified.
Gradual one-by-one replacement of old instances.
New version serves a small percentage of traffic first.
Traffic is mirrored to the new version whose responses are discarded.

check.q: A bank must release a backward-compatible bug fix with no downtime and has no budget for a second full environment. Which strategy fits?

items: Progressively replaces **V1 instances with V2**
**No downtime** or lost requests, **no extra resources**
What the lecture recommends for **bug fixes and patches**
a.foot: Needs enough **healthy capacity** while instances are swapped; **V1 and V2 must stay compatible**, because both serve traffic during the rollout and rollback.

check.q: A new fraud-detection model must be evaluated on real traffic without affecting any customer's decision. Canary or shadowing?

items: **Shadowing**: copies of requests go to V2 while customers get **V1's responses** → compare decisions without exposing anyone to the new model
**Canary** would let **5 to 10%** of customers be judged by an **unproven model**
a.foot: Shadowing needs **V2's writes and external side effects isolated**, because ignoring its response does not stop those from happening.

check.q: During a rolling update, V2 starts writing a new required column that V1 does not fill. A rollback to V1 then fails with errors. Which rule was broken?

items: **Rolling and canary** releases run old and new versions **side by side** and must allow **rollback**
→ Each new version must be **backward compatible** with existing data and callers
**Fix**: make the column **optional**, or give it a **default**, until every version that writes the table fills it
**Breaking changes** need **incremental releases** rather than one step

check.q: A major release must be switchable back within seconds if anything looks wrong, and the budget allows double capacity for a short time. Which strategy fits, and what does it not protect against?

items: V2 runs **alongside V1**; traffic switches only once V2 is confirmed working → switching back is **near-instant**
**Cost**: a second full environment for the duration
a.foot: **Does not protect against** data V2 has already written to **shared stores**: switching traffic does not undo it, so the data must stay **readable by V1**.

visuals.title: Traffic and rollback trade-offs
rows: Old or new environment after switch
Keep old environment ready; data must remain compatible
Isolate writes and other side effects

sections.title: Deployment case: splitting the Payment table
sections.summary: A breaking database change must be broken into backward-compatible increments (see the separate 05c case study).

items: **Payment microservice** stores all payment types in one **Payment** table
Analysis shows **Cheque** and **Apple Pay** capture different fields
So split the table into **ChequePayment** and **ApplePayPayment**
**Version 1** writes to Payment; **Version 2** writes to the two new tables
**Old data must be migrated**
The change is **not backward compatible** → old payments could not be read
notes.foot: The cure is **planning**: **incremental releases** 1.1, 1.2 ... finally **2.0**, each choosing a suitable deployment strategy.

terms.def: New version still works with old data and callers, enabling rollback.

check.q: V1 of the Payment service writes everything to one Payment table; V2 will write to ChequePayment and ApplePayPayment instead. Why can't this be done as a single rolling update to V2?

items: V2 cannot retrieve **historical payments** still in the Payment table
**Rolling update**: V1 and V2 share traffic → each would **miss the other's writes**
**Rolling back** would also hide payments V2 had accepted
a.foot: The lecture breaks it into **incremental releases** (1.1, 1.2, then 2.0) so each step stays compatible.

check.q: Step 1 of the case creates the two new tables with a rolling update and no code change. Why is this step safe, and why do it on its own?

items: **Safe**: no running code reads or writes the new tables yet → V1 is unaffected
**Rollback** just drops two empty tables
**On its own**: separates the **schema expansion** (database change) from any **behaviour change** → if a later step fails, the cause is easier to isolate
Later releases can rely on the tables **already existing**

sections.title: Circuit breaker
sections.summary: Stop a failing dependency from dragging callers down: fail fast, retry carefully, with the logic in an interceptor rather than business code.

notes.lead: Payment is down, or so slow that requests time out:
items: **Agency keeps calling** Payment
Agency's **thread pool clogs**
Agency can **no longer serve other calls**
**Requests to Agency clog** in turn
**Count** dependency errors or timeouts in a **window**
**Open** when a **threshold** is exceeded and **fail fast**
After a **reset interval**, allow **limited probes**
**Close only on success**
notes.foot: A **retry policy is separate**: use **bounded backoff** for transient failures without overwhelming recovery.

items: Coding forwarding/blocking logic into Agency is **not a business problem**
It would **change per protocol** (HTTP, gRPC, Thrift)

sub: track failures in a time window
retry some requests after the window

items: **Little or no code**

notes.h: Circuit breaker is a state machine
items: **Closed** → allow all
**Open** → deny all
**Half-Open** → allow some

terms.def: Interceptor that stops calls to a failing service and probes it again later.
Retry delays that double each time (50, 100, 200 ms ...).
One slow or failed service exhausting others' resources up the call chain.

check.q: The Payment service becomes extremely slow, and soon the Agency service stops answering even requests that never touch Payment. Explain why, and how a circuit breaker helps.

items: **Why**: Agency's **request threads** all block waiting on Payment → its **thread pool clogs** → it cannot serve anything
Its own callers then clog too → **cascading failure**

sub: Past a **threshold** → **opens** → fails calls to Payment **immediately**
Agency's threads stay free for other work

a.foot: Callers get an **error or fallback** for payment features until Payment recovers.

check.q: A team configures its circuit breaker with a reset timeout of zero and lets all traffic through once the breaker is half-open. What goes wrong?

items: **Half-open state** is meant to let **a few sample requests** test whether the dependency has recovered after a **rest period**
**No timeout + all traffic let through** → a recovering Payment service is **flooded** immediately → probably fails again
→ The breaker **flaps** between open and closed
**Fix**: give it a real interval, use **exponential backoff**, and send only a **subset** of requests while half-open

check.q: Developers plan to hand-code circuit-breaking logic around every outgoing call. Some services use HTTP and others gRPC. What would you suggest?

a.lead: **Use an interceptor** instead, through a **resilience library** or a **service mesh**.
items: Circuit breaking is **not a business problem**
Hand-written logic would need **rewriting for each protocol**
**Interceptor** tracks failures, opens the circuit and retries samples with **little or no code**
a.foot: **Cost**: another layer to configure and understand when debugging.

visuals.title: Circuit breaker state machine

steps.label: Closed
steps.detail: Normal state. Failures and timeouts are counted within a window.

steps.label: Open
steps.detail: Entered when failures or timeouts exceed the allowed limit. Callers get errors immediately without contacting the service.

steps.label: Half-Open
steps.detail: Entered when the reset timeout expires. If the sample requests succeed it goes back to Closed; if they fail, back to Open.

visuals.caption: Closed to Open when failures exceed limits; Open to Half-Open after the timeout; Half-Open to Closed on success or back to Open on failure.

sections.title: Rate limiting
sections.summary: Protect limited resources and spending by capping traffic per caller, again through interceptors.

items: **Not all users are equal** → conditional limits by plan
**Services have limited** CPU, memory and IOPS, and **limited budget**
**Unrestricted traffic invites DDoS**
An **interceptor** intercepts all requests
**Extracts** username, source IP, source service or user plan
Consults a **fast in-memory quota database** to verify and update limits and usage
notes.foot: **Little or no code.** Options: **Resilience4J, Sentinel, Istio, all cloud providers**.

items: **Circuit breaker** → protects the **caller** from a failing **callee**
**Rate limiter** → protects the **callee** from excessive **callers**

terms.def: Capping requests per caller, plan or source, enforced by an interceptor.

check.q: On a shared API, one free-plan user's script sends 10,000 requests a minute and slows the service for paying enterprise customers. What would you put in place?

items: Reads the **username, source IP, source service and plan** from each request → checks them against a **quota store**
**Free-plan** users get a lower limit than **enterprise** users → one script cannot take capacity from everyone
Also protects limited **CPU, memory and spending**
Blunts **denial-of-service** attempts

check.q: To avoid running another component, a teammate proposes keeping rate-limit counters in the main relational database. Do you agree?

items: The quota check runs on **every request** → must add **minimal latency**
Hence the lecture's **fast in-memory quota store**
**Counters in the main database** → a round trip and write load on every call → could slow the very service you are protecting
a.foot: The in-memory store must be **shared across instances**; briefly losing counts on a restart is usually acceptable for quotas.

check.q: A healthy service is being overloaded by one customer, while a different dependency is timing out. Which control fits each problem?

items: **Overloaded by one customer** → **rate-limit** the excessive customer, protecting the service's capacity for others
**Dependency timing out** → **circuit breaker** on it → callers stop waiting on it and **fail fast**
**Rate limiting** controls **incoming traffic volume**; a **circuit breaker** reacts to **failures of something you call**
a.foot: Using one in place of the other would not help.

sections.title: Distributed tracing
sections.summary: Follow one user request across many services using a shared ID, so failures are found quickly and MTTR drops.

notes.lead: One request touches many services; without tracing:
items: **Hard to debug**
**Slow fixes**, so **MTTR rises**
**Teams lose communication**
**Propagate a trace ID** in request headers across services
**Reuse incoming context**; create a **new trace at an entry point** when needed
**Instrumentation creates spans** and records **timing** and **parent/child relationships**
notes.foot: A **shared ID correlates work**; it does **not** make the request a single database transaction.

items: **Trace** → follows an end-to-end request
**Span** → records one unit of work, such as an HTTP call or database query
One service may produce **several spans**, so service count and span count need not match
**Jaeger** (CNCF)
**Spring Sleuth**
**Zipkin**
**Datadog**
**Stackdriver**

terms.def: End-to-end record of a request or business operation across components; not a database transaction.
Timed unit of work within a trace; one service can create several spans.
Mean time to recover.

check.q: A request enters through the gateway, which calls Order, which calls Payment. Payment generates a new UUID instead of reusing the incoming trace header. What breaks?

items: You can no longer follow the request from the **gateway to Payment**
A failure in Payment cannot be tied to the **user request** that caused it
**Rule**: only the **root creates the ID**; any service that finds the header populated **reuses** it
**Tracing libraries** enforce this by **intercepting requests** → safer than hand-written code in each service

check.q: Users report intermittent checkout failures spanning five services. The team spent two days logging into each container to find the failing one. What would cut that time?

items: **Distributed tracing** with a **shared trace ID** shows the **spans** for each request → the failing or slow service stands out
**Centralised logs** searched by that ID → the detail without logging into containers
**Untraceable problems** are what make **MTTR** rise significantly
a.foot: **Cost**: instrumenting services and running the tracing and logging back-ends.

check.q: In a 4-second checkout trace, the Payment span takes 3.8 seconds and contains a child span 'fraud-check' of 3.7 seconds. Where do you look first, and why does the child span matter?

a.lead: **Look at the fraud check first**: almost all of Payment's time is spent there.
items: **Span** = one unit of work
Services can create **child spans** through the **tracer API** to break their own work down
Without that child span → you would only know Payment was slow, not **which part**

sections.title: Distributed transactions and the Saga pattern
sections.summary: Why two-phase commit does not fit microservices, and how sagas use compensating transactions with orchestration or choreography.

notes.lead: They need consistency. The traditional answer is **two-phase commit** (**prepare**, then **commit**), but:
items: **Not all databases support ACID**
Platforms use **several databases**
**2PC needs synchronous communication**, while modern systems are **asynchronous**
notes.foot: **Skipping transactions is also risky**, because partial executions are dangerous.

items: **Commit local steps**; **compensate** completed steps after a later failure

sub: if payment fails: cancel MaidOrder, then Order

items: **Compensation is a new business action**, not an isolated database rollback
Compensation **may itself require retry**
**Orchestrator** → stores progress and directs forward and compensating steps; its **availability and contention** need attention
**Choreography** → distributes reactions among services; avoids one central controller but makes the **complete flow harder to debug**
A **shared traceId** is very important
**No read isolation** → users may read data from incomplete transactions or in-progress cancellations

terms.def: Business transaction made of local transactions with compensations, instead of 2PC.
Action that semantically undoes an earlier step (CancelPayment).
Prepare phase then commit phase; needs synchronous coordination.

check.q: Order data lives in a relational database and MaidOrder in a store without distributed-transaction support, and services talk asynchronously. A teammate proposes two-phase commit across them. Do you agree?

items: **Two-phase commit** needs **ACID-capable databases** and **synchronous communication**; this platform has neither
**Saga**: each service runs a **local transaction**
Each step **Ti** has a **compensating transaction Ci** that undoes it if a later step fails
a.foot: **Trade-off**: you give up atomic isolation in exchange for **loose coupling** and **asynchronous calls**.

check.q: In the Maid2Order saga, CreateOrder and CreateMaidOrder succeed, then MakePayment fails. What runs next, and in what order?

a.lead: The **compensations** for the completed steps run **in reverse**:
items: **1. CancelMaidOrder** in MaidOrderManager
**2. CancelOrder** in CustomerManager
**Asynchronous** like the forward steps → each compensation must be **safe to retry** and handle **duplicate messages**
A **shared trace ID** shows whether the whole saga, including compensation, completed

check.q: A customer sees a maid order as created, and a minute later it disappears because payment failed. Is this a bug?

items: **Sagas have no read isolation** → other users and screens can see data from transactions still **in progress** or **being compensated**
**Expect it and design for it**, e.g. show such orders as **pending** until the saga completes
If customers must **never** see unconfirmed orders → the read path has to **filter on saga state**

check.q: The team must debug failed orders quickly. Should the three-service order saga be orchestrated or choreographed?

items: **Orchestrator** holds the logic and publishes each **transaction and compensating event** → progress and failure points **visible in one place**
**Drawback**: can become a **single point of failure or contention** → must be made **highly available**
**Choreography** spreads logic across services → **harder to debug**
a.foot: Both still need **tracing** with a **shared trace ID**.

visuals.title: Payment failure reverses completed steps

steps.label: Create order
steps.detail: Commit the local order. CancelOrder is its compensating action.

steps.label: Create maid order
steps.detail: Commit the maid-service order. CancelMaidOrder compensates this step.

steps.label: Payment fails
steps.detail: The saga must correct already-completed work; local commits do not disappear.

steps.label: Compensate in reverse
steps.detail: Run CancelMaidOrder, then CancelOrder. These are new local transactions; observers may see intermediate state.

visuals.caption: A shared trace ID helps follow the flow; a saga provides no automatic read isolation.

sections.title: Metrics
sections.summary: What to measure (infra, application, availability) and the key formulas: uptime, nines, yield and harvest.

items: **Lower cost**
**Faster APIs**
**Better client retention** and service
**Meeting SLAs**
notes.foot: 'If you can't measure it, you can't improve it.'

items: **CPU and memory**
**Request volume** (IOPS)
**Availability**
**Peak usage time**
**Average response time**, with outliers and percentiles
**Success/failure rate**
**Payload sizes**
**Garbage collection time**
**Task success** → did the transaction finish or the customer drop out?
**Clarity** → ease of learning and use (heatmaps)
**Happiness** → returning visitors, visit frequency
**Lecture uses** → (MTBF − MTTR) / MTBF, treating **MTBF** as the complete failure-to-failure interval **including recovery**
**Worked example** → 1000 h between failures, 1 h recovery: 999/1000 = **99.9%**
If a problem defines **MTBF as operating time only** → use **MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)**
**State the convention**; the formulas are not interchangeable definitions
**Yield** = successful requests / total requests → measures **service actually received**
**Harvest** = available data / total data → measures **completeness**
notes.foot: A service can **stay up yet return errors or incomplete data**, so these measures answer different questions.

items: **Prometheus** time-series DB with **Grafana**
**TICK stack** → Telegraf, InfluxDB, Chronograf, Kapacitor
**Splunk metrics**
**Metrics-as-a-service**

terms.def: Fraction of time available; the lecture uses (MTBF − MTTR) / MTBF with the full interval in the denominator.
Successful requests divided by total requests.
Data available divided by total data.

check.q: A service fails on average every 500 hours and takes 2 hours to recover. Does it meet a 99.9% uptime target by the lecture's formula, and what would it take to meet it?

items: **To meet it** with the same failure rate: **MTTR** must fall to **0.5 hours**, since (500 - 0.5) / 500 = 99.9%
a.foot: So **faster recovery**, through tracing, central logs and quick rollback, is as much a lever as failing less often.

check.q: An API answers every request successfully but returns only half of the requested dataset because some data servers are down. What do yield and harvest show?

items: **Yield** = successful requests / total → **100%**, if those responses count as successful
**Harvest** = data available / total data → **50%**
Yield alone would **hide the problem** → define success according to **what users need** and report **both**
a.foot: Which matters more depends on whether a **partial answer** is useful to the user.

check.q: To show that an API meets 'responses within 3 seconds for 90% of requests', a teammate reports an average response time of 1.2 seconds. Does that show the target is met?

items: A mostly fast API can still have **well over 10%** of requests above **3 seconds**
Measure the **90th percentile** directly over a defined **window and load**
Hence the lecture lists **response time with outliers and percentiles**
Also report the **failure rate**: failed requests are not fast successes

check.q: A checkout API shows 99.99% yield and low latency, yet completed purchases have dropped by 20%. Which metrics would you look at?

items: **Task success**: do transactions end in success, or do customers **drop out**?
**Clarity**: how easily customers can use the product, e.g. through **heatmaps**
**Infrastructure metrics** show the API responds, not that users **complete what they came for**
**Happiness** signals such as **returning visitors** → whether the drop is lasting

visuals.title: Availability metrics
rows: Data completeness, not simply server count

sections.title: Logging, monitoring and summary
sections.summary: Centralised log aggregation patterns and how all the tools map to platform goals.

notes.lead: Engineers spend much of their time **debugging, analysing and tuning**. Typically log:
items: **Authentication/authorisation** successes and failures
**Changes to data entities**
**Access to external resources** (database, files, queues)
**Configuration**
**Application errors**
**Feature usage**

notes.lead: With many components, **one place to query and analyse** beats logging into every machine or container. Three shipping patterns:
items: **Direct** → app ships formatted logs directly to the central server
**Via transformer** → app ships raw logs to a transformation and shipping server that parses them into the central server's format
**Agent + parser** → app writes to a local file; a **lightweight shipping agent** sends raw logs to a remote parser; the **heavy transformer** stores into the central server
**ELK** (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) with **FluentD** or **Filebeat**
**Splunk**
**AWS centralised logging**
**Stackdriver**
**Papertrail**
**Loggly**
**Seamless interaction** → deployment strategies (rollout, canary)
**Scaling** → auto-scaling
**Limiting** → circuit breaker, rate limiting, retries
**Experimentation/traffic management** → canary
**Data-driven intelligence** → logs and metrics (observability)
**Faster issue resolution** → logging, monitoring and distributed tracing
notes.foot: **Security** (mutual TLS, reducing attack surface) is mentioned but not covered.

terms.def: Understanding system behaviour from collected logs, metrics and traces.
Lightweight process sending local log files to a remote parser (e.g. Filebeat).

check.q: Applications parse and format their logs before shipping them, and CPU on the application hosts has risen by 15%. What pattern would reduce this?

a.lead: **Ship raw logs, parse elsewhere** → parsing moves off the application hosts.
items: Write logs to a **local file**
A **lightweight shipping agent** sends **raw logs** to a separate, heavier **parser and transformer**
It stores them in the **central log server**
a.foot: **Cost**: another tier to run, and some **delay** before logs are searchable.

check.q: After an incident, the team cannot tell who changed a customer's bank details or when. What should have been logged, and where?

a.lead: **What** to log, all shipped to a **central log store**:
items: **Authentication and authorisation** successes and failures
**Changes to data entities**
**Access to external resources** such as databases and queues
**Why centralise**: the change may have passed through **several services**, and searching each container is slow
**Trace ID** in each entry → the whole change can be followed across services

check.q: In one incident, a partner floods the API, a downstream service fails slowly, and nobody can find where the errors start. Map each problem to the toolbox.

items: **Partner flood** → **rate limiting**
**Slow downstream service** → contain the slow dependency with a **circuit breaker**, **timeouts** and careful **retries**, which also limit the interaction
**Can't find where errors start** → **distributed tracing** plus **centralised logging and monitoring**, which lower **reaction time**
a.foot: Each tool addresses a different failure, so having one does not replace the others.

steps.label: Application
steps.detail: The app just writes raw logs locally.

steps.label: Shipping agent
steps.detail: Ships raw logs to a remote parser (e.g. Filebeat, FluentD).

steps.label: Parser / transformer
steps.detail: Parses logs and converts them to the central server's format (e.g. Logstash).

steps.label: Central log server
steps.detail: Single place to search logs across all components (e.g. Elasticsearch with Kibana).

exam_angles.q: A platform runs ten microservices on a container orchestrator, each auto-scaling from 2 to 20 instances. Design how services find each other, how that mechanism stays available, and what you would not build yourself.

items.t: **Finding each other**: callers refer to each service by **alias**, resolved through a **registry**
sub: Works like an **internal DNS**: instances **register**, callers **look up**, then **connect**
→ Scaling and restarts never require **configuration changes**

items.t: **Staying available**: a **consensus-backed cluster** of **three or five** nodes
**Don't build it yourself**: use the orchestrator's **built-in DNS discovery**
sub: Writing client and server discovery code takes engineers away from **business requirements**

a.foot: Discovery handles traffic **between services**; user traffic still enters through the **gateway**.

exam_angles.q: The Payment service becomes slow, and the Agency service, which calls it, starts failing all its requests. Identify the cause, propose a countermeasure, and give the countermeasure's main drawback.

sub: Agency's threads block waiting on Payment → its **thread pool clogs** → it cannot serve even unrelated requests

items.t: **Countermeasure**: a **circuit breaker** in an **interceptor**, through a **resilience library** or **service mesh**
sub: Goes **half-open** after an interval to send **sample requests**, with **exponential backoff**
Add **rate limiting** if Payment is overloaded by volume
While the circuit is **open**, payment-dependent features **fail fast or degrade** for every user
Badly tuned **thresholds** can open the circuit on **brief blips**

exam_angles.q: Choose a deployment strategy for (a) a routine, backward-compatible security patch; (b) a new recommendation model whose effect on user behaviour must be measured; (c) a major release that must be switchable back instantly. Justify each and give one shared precondition.

sub: **No downtime** and **no extra resources**, ideal for patches

items.t: **(b) Recommendation model → canary** with **5 to 10%** of traffic
sub: **Shadowing** would let you compare outputs without exposure but **cannot measure user reaction**
V2 runs **alongside V1** and traffic **switches back at once**

a.foot: **Shared precondition**: versions must stay **backward compatible with the data**, because switching traffic does not undo writes.

exam_angles.q: An order spans CustomerManager (CreateOrder), MaidOrderManager (CreateMaidOrder) and PaymentManager (MakePayment), each with its own database and asynchronous messaging. Design the consistency mechanism, its failure handling, and what users may observe.

a.lead: **Use a saga**, because **two-phase commit** needs **synchronous calls** and **ACID support** across all databases.
items: **Failure handling**: each step has a **compensation**; if MakePayment fails → run **CancelMaidOrder** then **CancelOrder**

sub: **Orchestrator** for central visibility, made **highly available** to avoid a **single point of failure**
or **choreography** for independent reactions, at the cost of **harder debugging**

items: **Trace** every step with a **shared trace ID**; make steps and compensations **idempotent**
**Users may see** in-progress or cancelled orders, because sagas have **no read isolation** → show such orders as **pending**

exam_angles.q: Over a 90-day quarter (2,160 hours), a platform had four failures, each taking 3 hours to recover. The SLA promises 99.9%. Using the lecture's metrics, does it comply, which metric matters most to users, and what would you change?

sub: **Uptime** = (540 - 3) / 540 = **99.44%** → misses 99.9% (about **9 hours** of downtime a year)

items.t: **Matters most to users: yield**, more than uptime
sub: An outage at **3 a.m.** with no traffic costs little, while one at **peak** costs many requests
So also report **successful over total requests** and the **harvest** of data served
To comply with the same failure rate → **MTTR** must fall to about **0.54 hours** → invest in **tracing**, **centralised logs** and **fast rollback**

exam_angles.q: Users report intermittent errors on a flow that crosses five services, and nobody can reproduce them. Which observability tools would you use, in what order, and what does each contribute?

sub: **Error rate** and **latency percentiles** per service → show **when** the errors happen and **which service's** numbers move
One ID **created at the root** and **propagated in headers**
Shows which **span** fails or slows in an affected request
**Child spans** narrow it down within a service
Searched by that **trace ID** → the **exception and context** without logging into each container

a.foot: Together they lower **MTTR**; **cost**: instrumenting every service and running the back-ends.
